The overall heat transfer resistance during drying includes resistance through the porous material and resistances from the condensate layer, dryer wall, and corrosion scale. During the heating process, almost no evaporation takes place as the material is wrapped in a dryer fabric and is pressed against the dryer surface. Evaporated water is mostly removed in between the dryer cans using low velocity air in the open draw/pockets where convective heat and mass transfer occurs. This process is repeated many times over the length of the dryer section. Conductive heating from one side, liquid water movement by capillary action, water vapor diffusion through the wet porous structure, and slow convective mass transfer in the pockets are all inherent limitations of the current technology and contribute to overall low efficiency. Increasing the efficiency of the dryer section is identified as a breakthrough in the reduction of energy intensity and will also advance productivity and quality. Reducing the thermal budget of drying process represents a significant opportunity and is a priority. Integration of cross cutting, electrically-powered technologies will directly impart the energy into the biomaterials resulting in high energy efficiency and higher throughput. The water removal from porous materials, the key technical challenge in paper manufacturing and other process industries, is addressed here by offsetting the evaporation load with a hybrid RF and US system (RFUS).The RFUS concept would enable the U.S. manufacturing industry to reduce capital and operating costs, energy consumption, and carbon emissions while increasing energy efficiency and throughput, improving product quality and sustainability, and helping preserve U.S. manufacturing jobs. The project explored the integration of modern approaches in process intensification for drying processes in conventional systems to develop a volumetric drying process (i.e., dries from inside out of the material) with high energy efficiency and high throughput. The hybrid drying approach incorporates directed radio frequency (RF) and ultrasonic (US) energy with conventional conduction, diffusion and convective heat and mass transfer overcoming the limitations of the conventional drying processes and that meets/exceeds the minimum goals as described below. Our concept is a powerful innovative hybrid volumetric drying technology integrating directed RF and US energy in conventional conductive and convective drying process. We target effective removal of free and bound water in the biomaterials by leveraging the synergies of RF and US technologies integrated with conventional manufacturing processes (Figure 1). 9 DE-EE0009395 Figure 1. Illustration of RF and US drying concepts Laboratory-scale experimental systems to evaluate the drying characteristics of paper and board drying often include discontinuous data acquisition methods with various assumptions. The majority of previous experimental drying research involved using either gravimetric measurements or using load cells to determine the water removal during drying, each of which have their own drawbacks. It should be noted that an experiment to track and acquire the behavior of alternating conduction and convection of a paper sample under close-to-commercial conditions, continuous movement of the sample and its subsequent disturbances would render using the load cells highly inaccurate.
